advisor.summary: Converting a profitable pass-through to C status is a rate-spread wager with a long-dated option attached. Profit the corporation retains is taxed once at the flat 21% rate of §11 instead of the owner's marginal stack, but every dollar distributed beyond salary picks up a second tax at qualified-dividend rates plus NIIT, and the §199A deduction on that income is forfeited entirely — which is why the engine models this as a strategy that can raise current burden, and the record honestly declares it. The structure wins for owners in the top brackets who genuinely reinvest, and the OBBBA-expanded §1202 exclusion — up to the greater of $15 million or 10x basis for post-July 4, 2025 issuances, with 50/75/100% tiers at three-, four-, and five-year holds — can convert the patience into a substantially tax-free exit for qualified businesses under the $75 million asset cap. The guardrails are the §531 accumulated earnings tax and §541 personal holding company regimes, and the door out is expensive: this is a structural commitment, not an annual election.
mechanics: The conversion path is mechanical: an LLC or sole proprietorship incorporates tax-free under §351 or checks the box on Form 8832, while an existing S corporation revokes or terminates its election; either way the owner becomes a W-2 employee and the business files Form 1120.

Retained profit is taxed at the flat 21% rate under §11 with no self-employment tax and no individual brackets — but also no §199A deduction, so the honest comparison is against the owner's effective pass-through rate after QBI, not the headline bracket.

Cash the owner takes beyond salary is a dividend under §§301 and 316, taxed again at qualified-dividend rates plus the 3.8% net investment income tax; at meaningful distribution levels the combined burden generally exceeds the pass-through alternative, which is exactly what the engine's dividend input demonstrates.

The §1202 exit thesis requires original-issuance C corporation stock in a qualified trade or business with aggregate gross assets of $75 million or less at issuance; for stock issued after July 4, 2025, P.L. 119-21 allows exclusion of the greater of $15 million or 10x basis, vesting 50% at a three-year hold, 75% at four, and 100% at five — and stock issued while an S election was in effect never qualifies, so the holding-period clock starts at conversion or later issuance, not at company founding.

Two penalty regimes police the retained-earnings story: the §531 accumulated earnings tax (20% on retention beyond documented reasonable business needs, above the $250,000 credit) and the §541 personal holding company tax (20% where passive income and concentrated ownership tests are met) — board-documented reinvestment plans are the defense file.

The engine removes the flow-through business, pays the entered salary as W-2 wages, charges 21% corporate tax on the remainder, and runs entered dividends through the personal return — deliberately surfacing the cases where conversion increases the current-year burden.

authority.note: The flat 21% corporate rate — the deferral spread against the owner’s marginal rate is the entire near-term case.
QSBS exclusion for post-July 4, 2025 issuances: $75M gross-asset cap, greater of $15M or 10x basis, and the 50/75/100% tiers at three-, four-, and five-year holds.
Distributions out of earnings and profits are dividends — the second tax layer, at qualified-dividend rates for domestic corporations.
The 20% accumulated earnings tax on retention beyond reasonable business needs — documented growth plans are the defense.
The 20% personal holding company tax — the trap for closely held corporations that drift into passive income.
Tax-free incorporation in exchange for stock — the transaction that starts the §1202 original-issuance and holding-period analysis.
The pass-through deduction forfeited on conversion — the offset that shrinks the apparent rate spread.

requirements: Sustained profitability with genuine reinvestment need — the structure only outruns a pass-through when cash actually stays in the business.
Owner marginal rates high enough that the 21% rate creates a real spread after losing §199A.

For the QSBS thesis: a qualified trade or business (service fields excluded under §1202(e)(3)), gross assets of $75 million or less at issuance, and stock issued while the corporation is a C corporation.
Reasonable W-2 compensation run through payroll and annual Form 1120 compliance.
Board-documented retention plans maintained as the §531 defense file from year one.
risks: The dominant failure mode is distribution reality: owners who need the cash personally pay the double tax, and the modeled dividend scenario frequently shows conversion increasing total burden — this record declares mayIncreaseBurden because that is the honest result.

The §531 accumulated earnings tax and §541 personal holding company tax are the classic exam theories against retained-earnings structures; hoarded cash without documented plans, or drift into investment income, invites a 20% surcharge.

Unwinding is expensive: appreciated assets exit a C corporation only through taxable distributions, and re-electing S status carries built-in-gain toll charges and waiting periods — treat the conversion as a five-to-ten-year commitment.

The §1202 exclusion is facts-heavy — original issuance, qualified-business status, the asset cap at issuance, and holding periods must be documented contemporaneously, because an exam five years later reconstructs all of it.
Losing §199A and the pass-through PTET deduction narrows the spread more than clients expect; the comparison must be run on the client's real numbers, which is what the model exists to do.
stateNotes: Conformity: Missouri conforms on a rolling basis, and its 4% corporate rate (RSMo §143.071) is among the lowest in the country — the combined federal-plus-Missouri corporate rate keeps the retention spread attractive for Missouri operating companies.

PTET interaction: conversion forfeits it — a C corporation cannot make a pass-through entity tax election, so the SALT-cap workaround the owner enjoyed as an S corporation or partnership disappears with the flow-through; this record conflicts with the PTET strategy by design.

Missouri: HB 594 (2025) lets individuals deduct 100% of federally reported capital gains from Missouri income, so a future stock sale — QSBS or not — is effectively Missouri-tax-free for individual sellers; a matching corporate subtraction activates only when the individual rate reaches 4.5%, so track the trigger.
reviewChecklist: Both scenarios modeled on the client's actual profit, salary, and distribution needs — including the dividend case that shows the structure losing.
Reasonable compensation set and documented for the post-conversion W-2, with payroll actually running.
QSBS documentation assembled at issuance where §1202 is part of the thesis: qualified-business analysis, gross-asset test, and holding-period calendar.
Retained-earnings plans recorded in board minutes as the §531 defense; passive-income mix screened against §541 annually.
PTET forfeiture and §199A loss included in the presented comparison.
Client has acknowledged in writing that the structure is a multi-year commitment with taxable exit ramps.

client.teaser: Profits you keep in the business can be taxed at a flat 21% — and a future sale might be largely tax-free.
client.headline: A flat 21% rate on reinvested profits, and a path to a tax-free exit
plainEnglish: Right now, every dollar your business earns lands on your personal return, even profit you never take out. Your personal rate can run well past 30%. As a regular corporation, profit the business keeps is taxed once, at a flat 21%.

That gap matters when you are reinvesting. Money kept in the company to hire, buy equipment, or build inventory grows from a bigger after-tax base each year. The catch: cash you pull out beyond your salary is taxed a second time. So this works best when the business, not your household, needs the money.

There is also a long-term prize. Hold the company's stock long enough, and current law can make a large part of a future sale tax-free — up to fifteen million dollars or more for qualifying companies. The clock starts when the structure is set up, which is a reason to decide early.
This is a big, structural move, and it is not right for everyone. We model your real numbers both ways first, because for owners who spend most of their profit, staying a pass-through usually wins.
client.analogy: Think of the corporation as a greenhouse for profits: money that stays inside grows in a better climate, but every trip out the door costs a toll — so we only build it for profits you truly mean to keep planted.
benefits: A flat 21% rate on profits kept in the business instead of your higher personal rate
More after-tax money compounding inside the company each year
A possible exit where a large share of the sale price is tax-free after five years
Missouri adds its own break: the state no longer taxes individuals on capital gains
steps: WE model your current setup against the corporate structure using your real profit and spending needs.
WE handle the conversion paperwork, payroll setup, and the day-one records the future sale rules demand.
YOU take your salary through payroll and route personal spending through it — not through company draws.
WE meet each year to set the keep-versus-distribute mix and document the reinvestment plan.
clientCommitments: Live on your salary — money pulled out beyond it gets taxed twice
Keep board minutes and reinvestment plans current with our help
Commit for the long haul; unwinding this structure is costly

annualMaintenance: Annual keep-versus-distribute review against the client's cash needs and the double-tax math
Update board minutes documenting retained-earnings plans (the accumulated-earnings defense)
Screen the passive-income mix against the personal holding company tests
Advance the QSBS holding-period calendar and refresh the qualification file
deliverables: Conversion decision memo modeling both structures on client facts
Incorporation / check-the-box filing package and payroll setup
QSBS qualification file: qualified-business analysis, gross-asset test at issuance, holding-period calendar
